meta.title: What the Letter Actually Names
meta.summary: The five CAGED letters name geometric shapes, not chords — barre the C form at the fifth fret and the chord you get is F.

spans.text: Barre the open
C
chord shape at fret 5 and most players will call the result a C. It isn't. It's
F

A barre is a movable nut. The open C chord only spells C because the guitar's real nut happens to put its root on string 5, fret 3. Swap that nut for a finger and the arrangement becomes portable — same skeleton, but the note it starts on now depends entirely on where you set the finger down.

You already know this trick in your hands, even without a name for it. The two barre chords everyone learns first — the one built from the open E chord and the one built from the open A chord — work exactly this way: hold the arrangement, move where the nut effectively falls, and the chord follows. CAGED is the same trick applied to five open chords instead of the usual two.
Play it out in full. Open C is
, strings 6 through 1. Barre that same shape at fret 5 and every finger moves up five frets together:
. The root — the note that used to sit on string 5, fret 3 — now sits on string 5, fret 8. That fret is
F
. Same shape, different chord, because the root landed somewhere else.

So the five letters in CAGED don't name five chords. They name five geometric arrangements — five ways a major chord's root, third and fifth can sit across six strings, each one worked out from a familiar open chord. Any one of those arrangements can spell any chord at all, C included, depending only on where the nut — real or movable — happens to be. Each is named after the open chord it resembles, C, A, G, E, D, which is where the acronym comes from — but the letter is a label for the skeleton, never a promise about the sound that comes out of it.

You'll see these five arrangements called shapes elsewhere in the guitar world — a fair synonym, and worth recognising when you meet it. This pathway calls them forms: the C form, the A form, and so on.

This chapter takes one chord — C — and finds where each of its five forms actually sits on the neck. For now you're marking only the root of each form: the single note that tells you which chord you're really holding. Everything else a form contains, its third and its fifth, waits for the next chapter. Roots first, because every other note gets measured from one — once you can find a form's root without counting, everything you add on top of it later slots into place around something solid.

That's the destination: every C on the neck, in all five forms, laid out as one picture. Don't try to read it yet — five overlapping bands is a lot to take in at once. Just notice C shows up again and again, and by the end of this chapter you'll know exactly why. Treat it as a preview: a promise that the pattern beneath these five shapes eventually clicks into one continuous map, not five separate ones.
The letter never tells you the chord. Only the root does — find that, and you know what you're actually playing.

the C form itself
, right where it was named — sitting at the nut.
